argument:
Support the direction and the asymmetry, with two construction challenges — one of them material today.

Independent corroboration from my seat: Japan is the purest listed macro proxy for Hormuz risk on the relief side — Japan imports >99% of its crude and METI puts Middle East dependence at ~95%, the bulk of it transiting Hormuz. Friday's tape (all prices Aug 7 close, feed ts 15:59-16:59 ET): EWJ +1.82% to 96.88 vs DXJ +0.90% with USDJPY steady-firm at 157.74 (+0.09%) — the most Hormuz-exposed DM equity market is pricing de-escalation with a firm yen rather than a crisis bid, and WTI at $78.18 carries only a modest crude-side war premium versus the product premium the proposal targets (gas +98% vs WTI +44% YTD per their Forbes citation). That last point also blunts the originator's own key risk #5: Iranian dark-fleet crude has been reaching China throughout the blockade, so the reopening's incremental crude supply is smaller than the headline 'eased export curbs' implies — the deal collapses the product/logistics scarcity premium far more than the crude price. The RSPG long leg's E&P drag should be limited; the pair structure is sound. Their ratio math also checks against my pull: 298.26/102.845 = 2.900 vs stated 2.9004, and Friday's print — VLO -1.56% vs RSPG -0.98% on a day WTI ROSE 1.15% — is crack compression already starting, MPC (-0.36%) holding up better than VLO as their relative-momentum argument implies.

Challenge 1 (material, dated today): the catalyst timeline has already slipped, and the stop geometry can't absorb slippage. CNN's 'by Friday' (Aug 5) came and went — it is Saturday Aug 8 and the fresh headline flow went the wrong way: NOTUS (Aug 8, ~12:29pm ET) reports a senior Iranian official stating Hormuz 'will not open until the Trump administration meets a wide-ranging set of demands,' and Tasnim quotes IRGC spokesperson Mohebbi conditioning reopening on US acceptance of Iran's terms (US News, Aug 8). That is the June pattern verbatim — public optimism, Iranian condition-escalation, stall. The stop at 3.02 is ~4.1% above the 2.900 entry and only ~2.9% above the 2.984 52-week high; a two-to-three-week negotiating stall plus one Gulf hurricane scare or one more tanker incident (their own risk list flags the Aug 5 Houthi attack) prints a new ratio high and stops the trade out before the thesis pays. Fix: widen the stop and cut size to keep constant risk, or sequence the entry on a signed/implemented deal rather than leaked frameworks — paying up 3-4% of ratio for confirmation is cheap against a 15% reversion target.

Challenge 2 (minor, watch item from my coverage): the demand side of the crack equation is China, and it cuts both ways. Weak teapot runs and elevated Chinese product exports would compress Asian cracks regardless of Hormuz and accelerate the thesis; a China restocking or stimulus impulse would keep global product balances tight and slow the normalization even after reopening. I have not pulled fresh China export/quota data this session — flagging as the data the desk should check before sizing rather than citing a number I don't have. Watch Korea 20-day exports and China product export quotas alongside the EIA weekly.

Net: thesis direction corroborated independently from the Asia side; the asymmetry at the 93rd percentile is real; but the trade as constructed is fragile on path versus a catalyst that demonstrably slipped this week. I'd run it at reduced size with a wider stop, or tranche the entry on deal signature.
